videos.title: Why Your Autonomous AI Data Agent Is Secretly An Idiot
videos.description:
You can have the most technically brilliant data team on the planet, but if they are just moving numbers around without driving actual business decisions, they are entirely useless . It is a harsh truth, but someone has to say it over a pint. We are obsessed with building massive data architecture. Yet we tolerate broken windows in our data warehouses, leaving tiny inconsistencies to fester until they infect every reporting tool in the company . We even have to build literal traffic lights on our dashboards just so executives know when the numbers are actually safe to look at. The shiny new solution is to throw artificial intelligence at the problem. We are seeing lightweight databases morph into the perfect local brains for swarms of autonomous agents . Tech giants are deploying context aware bots to crawl through petabytes of information, inferring semantics and writing code for us. But here is the punchline. If you unleash a highly capable bot into a swamp of undocumented and chaotic data, you have not solved your analytics problem. You have just built a machine that makes terrible decisions at unprecedented speed. The adults in the room are realising that these bots need strict boundaries. Smart companies are building rigorous metric semantic layers to enforce one single source of truth . Major cloud providers are constructing massive context graphs so these algorithms actually understand what they are looking at instead of just guessing. The role of the analytics engineer is fundamentally shifting away from writing basic queries to designing the overarching system and governing the bots. Grab a flat white and settle in, because we are breaking down exactly how to stop your data architecture from collapsing under its own weight.

videos.title: Is Open Source Dying? How AI Is Changing Software Development
videos.description:
Is open-source software still a sustainable strategy in the age of AI?

In this episode of Databased, Convex co-founders Jamie Turner and James Cowling examine how AI coding tools, large language models, and increasingly capable software agents are changing the economics of open-source software.

For developers, open source has historically been one of the best ways to learn how production systems work, explore software architecture, contribute to meaningful projects, and build new applications on top of shared infrastructure. However, AI models can now analyze large codebases, explain complex implementation decisions, generate competing software, and potentially recreate products without directly copying the original source code.

Jamie and James discuss whether this shift makes copyright, software licenses, patents, trade secrets, proprietary test suites, and operational expertise more important than they were before. They also explore why many successful open-source projects are funded by commercial companies, what happens when larger organizations use AI to replicate startup innovations, and why the team behind a codebase may still be more valuable than the code itself.

The conversation also covers Convex’s approach to source-available software, the Functional Source License, closed-source testing infrastructure, deterministic simulation testing, network effects, operational excellence, and the challenges of protecting a technical advantage while still contributing to the developer community.

Developers interested in open source, AI-assisted coding, backend infrastructure, databases, software licensing, startup strategy, full-stack development, distributed systems, and the future of software engineering will find a nuanced discussion about where the industry may be heading.
